title: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook
pub: New Media & Society, vol. 20, no. 1, pp. 293-310 (2018)
author: Jean-Christophe Plantin · Carl Lagoze · Paul N. Edwards · Christian Sandvig

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source analyzes the convergence of digital platforms and infrastructures, emphasizing privatization, programmability, interoperability, lock-in and corporate control. It does not address legal AI’s task-level capabilities, lawyer–AI division of labour, verification, user expertise or legal operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Platform governance: External innovation preserves gatekeeper power
st.an: The source accepts the core proposition that platforms invite third-party innovation while preserving owner control, and materially develops it through architectural mechanisms, cases of lock-in and interoperability constraints, and the broader account of platforms becoming privately governed infrastructure.
qs: The platform remains a centrally controlled and designed system (often under corporate control), but benefits from the innovations of a large penumbra of third-party developers.

The costs of this approach, as platform studies has shown, come in the form of constraints, constant revisions forced by platform updates, and lock-in to the platform’s conception of users, functionality, and design values.

st.t: Platform infrastructure: Convenience can deepen private control
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition by treating major platforms as increasingly essential infrastructure whose modularity and convenience benefit users and developers while enabling corporate control, lock-in, data extraction and dominance. It also situates this development within privatization and proposes scrutiny of the balance between public interest and corporate power.
qs: Yet the fact remains that control of the platform puts Google in an unparalleled position of dominance, increasing its power to shape lives as well as knowledge.

mo.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Innovation networks: Open anchors can sustain elites

kp.k: Infrastructure and platform studies provide complementary analytical lenses
kp.d: The authors develop a theoretical framework through literature synthesis and case studies of the Open Web, Facebook and Google, rather than examining AI or legal services directly. Infrastructure studies illuminates essential, widely shared systems and public value; platform studies explains how programmable corporate systems simultaneously enable and constrain participation. The authors argue that these are overlapping perspectives on the same phenomena, not necessarily distinct categories of objects.
qs: Through case studies of Google, Facebook, and the Open Web, we have shown that rather than distinguishing two entirely separate objects, these approaches instead offer different lenses on phenomena fundamental to everyday life in contemporary societies.

kp.k: Infrastructures depend on gateways, social practices and durability
kp.d: The infrastructure literature reviewed describes development from centrally controlled systems into networks and internetworks connected by technical and social gateways. Standards, user habits and organizational routines sustain these arrangements. Reliability and durability encourage dependence, while breakdown exposes that dependence; supposedly universal services can also structurally exclude particular populations.
qs: The network phase signals not only the involvement of many more actors but also growing social commitments manifested in, for example, explicit standards, user habituation, and organizational routines.

Dependency stems from the qualities of ubiquity, reliability, and especially durability; major infrastructures such as railroads, telephone networks, Linnaean taxonomy, and the Internet endure over many decades, even centuries.

kp.k: Platform modularity enables innovation while concentrating control
kp.d: Drawing on management and media scholarship, the authors describe platforms as relatively stable cores linked through interfaces to variable complementary components. This architecture can reduce innovation costs and allow third parties to extend systems beyond their designers' intentions, but participation remains constrained by platform owners' commercial objectives.
qs: Such architecture can lower the cost of innovation because it avoids building an entirely new system for each new product (Baldwin and Woodward, 2008: 8–9).

Collectively, they highlight how platforms’ affordances simultaneously allow and constrain expression, as well as how technical, social, and economic concerns determine platforms’ structure, function, and use.

kp.k: Platform builders govern external ecosystems rather than internalizing production
kp.d: The authors distinguish platform builders from the system builders described in historical infrastructure studies. Platforms attract independent developers who benefit from code, standardized interfaces, audiences and marketing, while owners gain buy-in and lock-in. Developers bear constraints, repeated adaptation to updates and the cost of maintaining products across incompatible platforms.
qs: unlike system builders, platform builders do not seek to internalize their environments through vertical integration.
Instead, their platforms are designed to be extended and elaborated from outside, by other actors, provided that those actors follow certain rules.
This strategy forces independent developers either to commit to just one platform or to build and maintain multiple versions of the same product.

kp.k: Corporate interfaces connect expression to commercial data extraction
kp.d: Reporting platform scholarship, the authors explain that communicative actions such as liking, sharing and retweeting serve both user expression and ranking, recommendation and analytics. They also report Gillespie's argument that companies use the term platform to present themselves as neutral intermediaries and downplay their influence over public discourse.
qs: For example, “like,” “share,” and “retweet” not only provide a means for users to express themselves but also facilitate ranking, product recommendations, and data analytics.
For example, corporations’ goal of gathering users’ personal data determines the technical properties of platforms, which in turn shapes how they organize communication among users.

kp.k: Privatization and digital technologies jointly facilitate platformization
kp.d: The authors locate platform growth in the erosion, beginning in the late 1970s, of the ideal of universally available infrastructure supplied or regulated in the public interest. They argue that deregulation and privatization fragmented services, sometimes improving efficiency while leaving poorer citizens with inferior provision. Their computing history traces a shift from publicly supported computer-utility models toward privatized, commercially accessible networks, including Internet backbone privatization from 1987 and removal of commercial-use restrictions from 1992.
qs: Starting in the late 1970s, however, the modern infrastructural ideal began to collapse as neoliberal leaders sought to lower costs through market competition.

Digital technologies greatly assisted in this process, often making possible lower cost, more dynamic, and more competitive alternatives to governmental or quasi-governmental monopoly infrastructures, in exchange for a transfer of wealth and responsibility to private enterprises.

kp.k: The Open Web combines infrastructure with open programmability
kp.d: The authors describe HTTP, URIs, HTML and hyperlinks as publicly accessible, communally regulated foundations enabling publication, access and reuse. These standards make heterogeneous resources interoperable and allow application development without a single corporate gatekeeper. Openness concerns technical and institutional access, not necessarily free content. Their historical comparison notes that earlier proprietary dial-up services ultimately abandoned closed approaches when competing with the Open Web's variety.
qs: All of these components exist as publicly accessible, communally regulated standards (Fielding et al., 1999).
The Web creates interoperability among a huge variety of distributed, heterogeneous computers and content resources.
Open Web–based resources need not be free

kp.k: Facebook APIs enable extensions while restricting openness
kp.d: The authors characterize Facebook's API as both an infrastructural gateway and a mechanism of proprietary control. It enables independently developed applications to exchange data with Facebook but places developers and users within Facebook-defined boundaries. They explicitly note that APIs are not inherently commercial or closed, since governmental open-data initiatives also use them. Potential migration of news content into Facebook is presented conditionally, not as an established complete displacement of the Open Web.
qs: APIs are not used exclusively in commercial platforms; they are an increasingly common protocol in governmental open data initiatives.
On one hand, it increases the functionality of the Facebook platform by enabling an ecology of apps using the API to exchange data with Facebook.
Rather than connecting them to the Open Web, the API locks both groups into a landscape defined and controlled by Facebook,

kp.k: Facebook's embeddedness expands data collection and communicative power
kp.d: The authors report Facebook having an over 60% share of all social media transactions worldwide at the time discussed and interpret its reach and everyday embeddedness as emerging infrastructural status. Authentication through Facebook and connected applications contribute behavioral information to user profiles, including actions not deliberately undertaken as Facebook activity. The authors argue that this supports advertising, newsfeed customization and increasing influence over communication.
qs: With an over 60% share of all social media transactions worldwide, Facebook looks more and more like a de facto infrastructure.
For example, when users authenticate to websites or applications using their Facebook identities, the API records these acts to their Facebook data profiles.
Facebook then uses these data traces to tailor advertising and adjust newsfeed priorities, among other customizations to our personalized walled gardens.

kp.k: Google's search and applications create infrastructural dependence
kp.d: At the time of writing, the authors report Google accounting for over 65% of worldwide web searches, compared with Bing at 13% and Baidu and Yahoo at 9% each; they give Google's shares as 85% in the United States and 92% in Europe. These are historical figures reported by the article, not current estimates. They argue that search and integrated services make Google widely relied upon, including by businesses and universities replacing multiple legacy products, and that disappearance of those services would cause substantial disruption.
qs: At the time of this writing, Google accounts for over 65% of all web searches worldwide, trailed by Bing (13%), Baidu, and Yahoo (9% each).
This lopsided tally falls even more heavily in Google’s favor in the United States (85%) and Europe (92%).
These services have drawn Google’s users into ever deeper reliance on its services.

kp.k: Google Maps illustrates knowledge becoming a programmable resource
kp.d: The authors contrast earlier digital cartography, hindered by specialized software, cost, technical complexity and copyright, with Google's 2005 release of Maps and its API. Third parties could overlay information on Google's base map to create mashups. This enabled reuse and application development while returning user-activity data and extending Google's branded interface.
qs: In 2005, Google released Google Maps and almost immediately provided an API.
In other words, Google transformed maps into programmable objects, with Google Maps as the platform.

As with Facebook, the principal benefits to Google are the user activity data returned by the API and the ubiquity of its branded interface, while the myriad applications connected to the Google platform benefit from the ability to build on Google-provided data.

kp.k: Search control gives private platforms power over visibility
kp.d: The authors argue that Google's control over search creates substantial influence over which resources users encounter. They acknowledge Google's efforts to prevent manipulation and attribute to Google the assertion that payment cannot improve ranking except through labeled sponsored links. Nonetheless, they identify search optimization and profit-driven concentration as concerns, while discussing other search platforms as potentially permitting greater outside influence.
qs: Because it designs and controls Internet search, the company holds enormous power over the visibility of web-based resources.
Some companies’ entire business consists of helping others improve their position in Google search results.

kp.k: Google Books exposes tensions in privately supplied knowledge infrastructure
kp.d: The authors describe Google's university digitization partnerships beginning in 2004, its 2009 acquisition of reCAPTCHA partly to crowdsource difficult character recognition, and its Books API. They recognize potential benefits for discovery, underserved regions and developers, but interpret the project as an attempt to platformize libraries. Its universal-library promise remained unfulfilled at the time discussed amid lawsuits; the authors emphasize the trade-off between private execution capacity and concentrated control.
qs: Starting in 2004, Google partnered with major research universities to digitize “every” book.
It also released a Google Books API (with its attendant two-way flow of data) and allowed researchers to build applications on top of it.
Yet the fact remains that control of the platform puts Google in an unparalleled position of dominance, increasing its power to shape lives as well as knowledge.

kp.k: Research should examine public value alongside ecosystem power
kp.d: The authors recommend comparative historical and critical research on rapidly infrastructuralizing platforms and on infrastructures reorganized through platform strategies. Proposed applications include scholarly communication platforms and private systems used in smart-city administration. Their normative conclusion calls for attention to universal access, stability, exclusion and policy alternatives rather than treating platform profits and user benefits as interchangeable with public interest.
qs: The question is not only who profits and controls, but who, and what, is cast aside along the way.
In all cases, scholars of infrastructure could attend to the technological influences and policy alternatives that tip the delicate balance between the public interest and corporate power.
This combined perspective, one might hope, would reassert the importance of widely available, universal, and relatively stable infrastructure as a foundation of social justice.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Plantin, Lagoze, Edwards and Sandvig argue that digital platforms are becoming essential infrastructures while existing infrastructures are being reorganized around privately controlled platform models.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about digital media and knowledge infrastructures, not a source making claims about AI or legal services. The authors argue that platform architectures enable third-party innovation while creating lock-in, constraints and corporate control. Facebook's API expands its ecosystem while concentrating control over communication and user data. Google's search, applications, Maps and Books combine widely useful knowledge services with proprietary control over access, visibility and development. The authors also make a conditional prediction that Facebook-hosted news could move content away from openly addressable web resources into a restricted platform ecosystem.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is a theoretical synthesis supported by historical accounts, illustrative case studies and contemporaneous market-share figures, rather than AI benchmarks or legal-sector data.
pts.d: The authors combine infrastructure and platform scholarship with case studies of the Open Web, Facebook and Google. Their historical account traces publicly supported computing and networking through privatization and deregulation. Their platform examples include Facebook authentication and API-mediated data collection, Google's 2005 Maps API, and Google Books' digitization effort, API and litigation. They report Facebook's share as over 60% of worldwide social-media transactions and Google's worldwide search share as over 65%, with 85% in the United States and 92% in Europe. The Google figures are linked in notes to NetMarketShare and Experian; the Facebook figure has no explicit supporting citation at that point in the supplied text. These are figures reported at the time of writing, not current measurements. The potential displacement of openly accessible news content is presented as a prospective scenario, supported by reporting about Facebook's negotiations with publishers, not as an established measured outcome.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The argument concerns historical change from the late 1970s through the authors' mid-2010s writing context, with conditional future developments rather than dated forecasts.
pts.d: Although the supplied publication heading identifies the journal article as 2018, the document carries a 2016 preprint footer and uses mid-2010s sources. The authors connect infrastructure fragmentation to neoliberal reforms beginning in the late 1970s, Internet backbone privatization from 1987 and commercial-use deregulation from 1992, followed by Web 2.0 platform expansion. Platforms acquire infrastructure-like qualities when they become widely shared, embedded and difficult to do without; the authors do not claim that every platform necessarily becomes infrastructure. The news-content prediction depends explicitly on Facebook's hosting strategy succeeding. Google Books' universal-library promise is described as unrealized at the time of writing. Potential applications of the framework to scholarly communication and smart cities are suggestions for further research, not demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Users, independent developers, publishers, knowledge institutions and disadvantaged populations receive benefits but also face dependencies, restrictions and uneven access.
pts.d: Users gain convenient, integrated services but become dependent on corporate systems and subject to data collection and communication filtering. Independent developers can reuse platform code and data, reducing duplicated effort, but face update burdens, restricted interoperability and lock-in. Publishers risk shifting from independently accessible websites to platform-controlled distribution. Businesses and universities increasingly rely on Google's application suite, while libraries and researchers face a tension between expanded digital knowledge access and private control. Low-income populations can remain excluded where essential connectivity is provided through fragmented commercial markets. These are claims about digital inclusion and public infrastructure, not legal access to justice.
